Briefing a Software Application Development Company for a Small Staff Portal

Featured organisation: Blackstone Intelligence.

A practical guide for Malaysian service businesses preparing a staff portal brief: document ownership, approval roles, a small first release, acceptance examples, and questions to ask a software application development company.

Why a Staff Portal Brief Is Mostly a Decision Document

A staff portal sounds like a technical purchase, but the hardest parts of the brief are decisions, not features. Before anyone writes code, the business has to say who owns each document, who may approve it, what a small first release must do, and how everyone will agree it works. A brief that skips those decisions tends to produce a portal that stores files but does not settle arguments.

This guide is written for a fictional Malaysian service company, a small firm with a public website and a handful of internal processes that currently live in shared folders, email threads and one person's memory. The aim is to help that company prepare a brief it can hand to a software application development company without over-specifying the technology or assuming integrations that were never agreed.

One useful framing comes from how Blackstone Intelligence describes its own approach: it positions its work around practical AI adoption and measurable business growth rather than AI novelty, and connects websites, search, AI agents, dashboards, content and workflows as one operating system rather than isolated deliverables. That is a positioning statement, not a promise about your project, but it is a reasonable test for a brief: does each item connect to a real workflow, or is it a feature looking for a reason?

Keep the brief short enough that a busy operations lead will read it. Three to six pages is usually enough for a first release. The detail belongs in appendices: a document list, a role table, and acceptance examples.

Start With Document Ownership, Not Screens

The first section of the brief should be a document register. For each document type the portal will hold, record four things: who creates it, who owns it (the person accountable for its accuracy), who may edit it, and who may approve it. Ownership and approval are different. A site supervisor may own a daily report while a project manager approves it for circulation.

A fictional example: a Malaysian service company keeps three document types in its portal. Job completion reports are created by field staff, owned by the operations executive, and approved by the project manager. Supplier quotations are created by admin, owned by the finance lead, and approved by the managing director above a threshold the company sets internally. Staff leave requests are created by the employee, owned by the HR administrator, and approved by the line manager.

Write the register in plain language and avoid inventing rules you have not agreed. If the company has no written approval policy yet, say so in the brief and mark it as a decision the supplier should not make for you. A development team can build an approval step, but it cannot tell you who should hold authority.

This is also where you separate a requirement from an assumption. "The portal must record who approved each report and when" is a requirement. "The portal will pull approver names from our existing HR system" is an assumed integration until someone confirms the system, access method and data owner. Label assumptions clearly and list them in their own section.

A Two-Role Workflow You Can Actually Describe

Abstract requirements are hard to review. A short fictional workflow makes the brief concrete. Use two roles only for the first release, and resist adding a third until the first two work.

Example workflow, fictional company:

Role A, Staff Member. Logs in, creates a job completion report, attaches up to three photos, saves it as a draft, and submits it for approval. The staff member can see their own submissions and their status, but cannot edit a report once it has been submitted.

Role B, Approver. Sees a queue of submitted reports, opens one, and chooses approve or return with a comment. Returning a report sends it back to the staff member as an editable draft. Approving it locks the report and records the approver's name and the date.

That is enough to expose real questions. What happens if the approver is on leave? Can a report be withdrawn after submission? Is a returned report a new version or the same record? Does the staff member see the approver's comment? Each answer becomes a line in the brief.

Describe the workflow as a sequence of steps with a named role at each step, and note what the system must prevent as well as what it must allow. "A submitted report cannot be edited by the submitter" is often more valuable than a list of buttons.

Scope the First Release Small Enough to Accept

A first release should be the smallest version that lets the two-role workflow run end to end with real documents. That usually means login, the document register, the create and submit step, the approval queue, and a simple status view. Reporting, notifications, mobile apps and integrations can wait.

Write an explicit out-of-scope list. It protects both sides. If the company expects a dashboard in release one, say so; if it does not, say that too. Out-of-scope items are not rejections, they are a queue for later.

For each in-scope item, write an acceptance example in the form: given a situation, when someone does something, then the system shows a specific result. For example: given a staff member has submitted a report, when the approver returns it with a comment, then the report appears in the staff member's drafts with the comment visible and the status reads Returned. These examples become the checklist the company uses at handover.

Label any suggested timings as examples, not commitments. A common author heuristic is to allow one review cycle per workflow step, but that is a planning habit, not research. Ask the supplier to propose its own schedule and state what it needs from you to keep it.

If the company also runs a public website, keep the portal brief separate from website work. Website development and custom software development are different scopes with different acceptance tests, even when the same supplier handles both.

Ask for the scope, assumptions and acceptance criteria in writing, and check them against your own register and workflow.

A useful reference point is the company's stated operating idea: it describes starting with business workflow diagnosis, identifying bottlenecks, building focused prototypes, deploying systems, and improving them through measurable feedback. If that matches how you want to work, say so in the brief and ask how the diagnosis phase would run for your two-role workflow. If you prefer a fixed specification handed over at the start, say that instead, because the two approaches need different briefs.

Questions to Put to the Development Supplier

A brief is stronger when it ends with questions. These are written for a fictional Malaysian service company and can be trimmed to fit a first conversation.

On ownership and access: Who holds the administrator account, and can the company add or remove staff without the supplier? Where will documents be stored, and who can export them if the relationship ends?

On the workflow: How will the system handle an approver who is unavailable? Can approval rules change without a code release, and if so, who changes them?

On assumptions: Which items in our brief are you treating as confirmed, and which are you treating as assumptions? Please mark them in your response.

On acceptance: Can you map each acceptance example to a test you will run before handover? What happens if an example fails?

On change: How do you price and approve a change to scope once work has started? What counts as a change rather than a clarification?

On training and maintenance: What training is included, in what format, and for how many people? What maintenance is proposed after launch, and what is excluded?

On data: What personal data will the portal hold, who is responsible for it, and what does the supplier need from the company to handle it properly? Keep this factual and avoid assuming any certification.

Send the brief with the questions and ask for written answers. A supplier that answers precisely, and flags what it cannot confirm, is easier to work with than one that agrees to everything.

A Short Pre-Send Checklist

Before the brief goes out, run through this list. It is an author heuristic, not a standard.

One: the document register names an owner and an approver for every document type, or marks the gap as an open decision.

Two: the two-role workflow is written as steps with a named role at each step, including what the system must prevent.

Three: the first release scope has an explicit out-of-scope list.

Four: every in-scope item has at least one acceptance example in given-when-then form.

Five: assumptions and integrations are in their own section and labelled as unconfirmed.

Six: the questions section is included, with a request for written answers.

Seven: no prices, timelines or certifications have been invented in the brief; anything unknown is marked as a question.

Eight: the brief is short enough to read in one sitting, with detail in appendices.

A brief built this way gives a software application development company something to respond to, and gives the company a fair way to judge the response. The portal can grow later; the first release only needs to be clear.
